'''''Araucaria''''' ({{IPAc-en|pron|æ|r|ɔː|ˈ|k|ɛər|i|ə}}; original pronunciation: [a.ɾawˈka. ɾja])<ref>{{OED|araucaria}}</ref> is a [[genus]] of [[evergreen]] [[conifer]]ous trees in the family [[Araucariaceae]]. While today they are largely confined to the [[Southern Hemisphere]], during the [[Jurassic]] and [[Cretaceous]] they were globally distributed. There are 20 [[extant taxon|extant]] [[species]] in [[New Caledonia]] (where 14 species are [[endemism|endemic]], see [[New Caledonian Araucaria|New Caledonian ''Araucaria'']]), eastern [[Australia]] (including [[Norfolk Island]]), [[New Guinea]], [[Argentina]], [[Brazil]], [[Chile]] and [[Uruguay]].

The genus is familiar to many people as the genus of the distinctive Chilean pine or monkey-puzzle tree (''[[Araucaria araucana]]''). No distinct vernacular name exists for the genus. Many are called "pine", such as the "Norfolk pine" (''[[Araucaria heterophylla]]'') although they are only distantly related to true pines, in the genus ''[[Pinus]]''.

==Description==

''Araucaria'' are mainly large trees with a massive erect stem, reaching a height of {{convert|5|-|80|m}}. The horizontal, spreading branches grow in whorls and are covered with leathery or needle-like [[leaf|leaves]]. In some species, the leaves are narrow, awl-shaped, and lanceolate, barely overlapping each other; in others, they are broad and flat, and overlap broadly.<ref name="gymdb"/>

The two South American species ''[[Araucaria angustifolia|A. angustifolia]]'' and ''A. araucana'' are mostly [[Dioecy#In botany|dioecious]], with male and female [[Conifer cone|cones]] found on separate trees. The other species in the genus are [[Monoecy|monoecious]].<ref>[https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00606-012-0631-7 Genome sizes of all 19 Araucaria species are correlated with their geographical distribution]</ref><ref>[https://www.conifers.org/ar/Araucaria.php The Gymnosperm Database – Araucaria]</ref> The female cones, on the top of the tree, are [[globose]], and vary in size among species from {{convert|7|to|25|cm|frac=2}} in diameter. They contain 80–200 large [[Eating|edible]] seeds, similar to [[pine nut]]s, though larger. The male cones are smaller, {{convert|4|-|10|cm|abbr=on|frac=4}} long, narrow to broad cylindrical, and {{convert|1.5|-|5|cm|abbr=on|frac=4}} broad.

==Taxonomy==
The genus is named after the Spanish [[exonym]] ''Araucano'' ("from [[Arauco Province|Arauco]]") applied to the [[Mapuche]] of south-central [[Chile]] and south-west [[Argentina]], whose territory incorporates natural stands of a species in this genus identified as ''[[Araucaria araucana|A. araucana]]''; the Mapuche people call it ''{{lang|arn|pewen}}'', and consider it sacred.<ref name="gymdb"/> Some Mapuche living in the Andes name themselves [[Pewenche]] ("people of the ''{{lang|arn|pewen}}''") as they traditionally harvested the seeds extensively for food.<ref name="ntbg">{{cite web|url=http://ntbg.org/plants/plant_details.php?plantid=867|title=''Araucaria columnaris''|publisher=[[National Tropical Botanical Garden]]|access-date=19 November 2011|archive-date=16 June 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120616174201/http://ntbg.org/plants/plant_details.php?plantid=867|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name="moreno">{{cite web |url=http://www.bariloche.com.ar/museo/MAPUING.HTM |title=Pehuenches: "The people from the Araucarias forests" |author=Francisco P. Moreno |date=November 2004 |publisher=Museo de la Patagonia |access-date=18 November 2011 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120111130857/http://www.bariloche.com.ar/museo/MAPUING.HTM |archive-date=11 January 2012 }}</ref>

There are four extant [[section (botany)|sections]] and two extinct sections in the genus, sometimes treated as separate genera.<ref name="gymdb"/><ref name="black">{{cite book |author1=Michael Black |author2=H. ===Genetic studies===
[[File:Petrified Araucaria cone from patagonia-Edit3.jpg|thumb|Petrified cone of ''[[Araucaria mirabilis]]'' from [[Patagonia]], [[Argentina]] dating from the [[Jurassic|Jurassic Period]] (approx. 157 [[mya (unit)|mya]])]]

Genetic studies indicate that the extant members of the genus can be subdivided into two large [[clade]]s – the first consisting of the [[section (botany)|sections]] ''Araucaria'', ''Bunya'', and ''Intermedia''; and the second of the strongly [[monophyletic]] section ''Eutacta''. Sections ''Eutacta'' and ''Bunya'' are both the oldest taxa of the genus, with ''Eutacta'' possibly older.<ref name="setoguchi">{{cite journal |author1=Hiroaki Setoguchi |author2=Takeshi Asakawa Osawa |author3=Jean-Cristophe Pintaud |author4=Tanguy Jaffré |author5=Jean-Marie Veillon |year=1998 |title=Phylogenetic relationships within Araucariaceae based on ''rbcL'' gene sequences |journal=[[American Journal of Botany]] |volume=85 |issue=11 |pages=1507–1516 |pmid=21680310 |doi=10.2307/2446478|jstor=2446478 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

==Distribution and paleoecology==
[[File:Three araucarias.jpg|thumb|Three members of the genus growing together – left to right, ''[[Araucaria columnaris|A. columnaris]]'', ''[[Araucaria cunninghamii|A. cunninghamii]]'' and ''[[Araucaria bidwillii|A. bidwillii]]'']]

Members of ''Araucaria'' are found in [[Argentina]], [[Brazil]], [[New Caledonia]], [[Norfolk Island]], [[Australia]], [[New Guinea]], [[Chile]] and [[Papua (Indonesia)]].<ref>[http://everything-everywhere.com/2011/05/21/the-pine-trees-of-lanai/ The Pine Trees of Lanai]</ref> Many if not all current populations are [[Relict (biology)|relict]]s, and of restricted distribution. They are found in [[forest]] and [[maquis shrubland]], with an affinity for exposed sites. The earliest records of the genus date to the [[Middle Jurassic]], represented by ''[[Araucaria mirabilis]]'' of Argentina, and ''Araucaria sphaerocarpa'' from England. [[Fossil]] records show that the genus also formerly occurred in the northern hemisphere until the end of the [[Cretaceous]] period.<ref name=":0" /> A possible species of ''Araucaria'' may have existed in [[New Zealand]] as recently as 350,000 years ago.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal|last=Pole |first=Mike |date=2019 |title=A survey of Pliocene to Mid-Quaternary leaf cuticle from the North Island, New Zealand |url=https://doi.org/10.26879/862 |journal=Palaeontologia Electronica |volume=22 |issue=1 |doi=10.26879/862 |issn=1094-8074|doi-access=free }}</ref> However, it is also possible that this fossil actually represents a specimen of [[Agathis]].<ref name=":1" />

By far the greatest diversity exists in [[Geography of New Caledonia|New Caledonia]], likely due to a relatively recent [[adaptive radiation]], as all [[New Caledonian Araucaria|New Caledonian species]] are more closely related to each other than they are to other ''Araucaria''.<ref name=":0" /><ref name="gymdb">{{cite web|url=http://www.conifers.org/ar/Araucaria.php |title=''Araucaria'' Jussieu 1789 |author=Christopher J. Earle |date=12 December 2010 |publisher=The Gymnosperm Database |access-date=13 November 2011}}</ref> Much of New Caledonia is composed of [[ultramafic]] rock with [[serpentine soil]]s, with low levels of nutrients, but high levels of metals such as [[nickel]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://newcaledoniaplants.com/plant-catalog/maquis-shrubland-plants/|title=Maquis plants|date=October 13, 2013}}</ref> Consequently, its endemic ''Araucaria'' species are adapted to these conditions, and many species have been severely affected by [[nickel mining in New Caledonia]] and are now considered threatened or endangered, due to their habitat lying in prime areas for nickel mining activities.

Some evidence suggests that the long necks of [[sauropod]] dinosaurs may have evolved specifically to browse the foliage of tall trees, including those of ''Araucaria''. An analysis of modern ''Araucaria'' leaves found that they have a high energy content but are slow fermenting, making their ancestors a likely attractive target.<ref name="hummel">{{cite journal |author1=Jürgen Hummel |author2=Carole T. Gee |author3=Karl-Heinz Südekum |author4=P. Martin Sander |author5=Gunther Nogge |author6=Marcus Clauss |year=2008 |title=In vitro digestibility of fern and gymnosperm foliage: implications for sauropod feeding ecology and diet selection |journal=[[Proceedings of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences]] |volume=275 |issue=1638 |pages=1015–1021 |doi=10.1098/rspb.2007.1728 |pmid=18252667 |pmc=2600911 }}</ref> However, a diet consisting solely of ''Araucaria'' may not have provided dinosaurs with sufficient protein and was therefore unlikely. <ref>{{Cite book |last=Gee |first=Carole T. |title=Plants in Mesozoic time: morphological innovations, phylogeny, ecosystems |date=2010 |publisher=Indiana University Press |isbn=978-0-253-35456-3 |series=Life of the past |location=Bloomington|pages=350-351|chapter=Mesozoic Plants and Dinosaur Herbivory}}</ref>
   


==Uses==
{{Further| Araucaria angustifolia#Uses | A. araucana#Uses | A. bidwillii#Uses}}
Some of the species are relatively common in cultivation because of their distinctive, formal symmetrical growth habit. Several species are economically important for [[timber]] production.

===<span class="anchor" id="Nuts"></span>Food===
{{broader|Conifer nuts}}
The edible large seeds of ''A. araucana'', ''A. angustifolia'' and ''A. bidwillii'' — also known as '''''Araucaria'' nuts''',<ref>{{cite encyclopedia |title=Pine nut |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=TOG-ItIHp_kC&q=araucaria+nuts&pg=PA280 |encyclopedia=The Visual Food Encyclopedia |editor=Québec Amerique |date=1996 |page=280|isbn=9782764408988 }}</ref> and often called, although improperly, ''[[pine nuts]]'' — are eaten as food, particularly among the [[Mapuche]] people of Chile and southwest Argentina, the [[Kaingang]] people in [[Southern Brazil]] and among [[Indigenous Australian]]s.<ref name="gymdb"/>
In South America, Araucaria nuts or seeds are called ''piñas'' or ''piñones'' in Spanish and ''pinhões'' in Portuguese, like pine nuts in Europe.

===Pharmacological activity===
Pharmacological reports on the genus ''Araucaria'' are [[anti-ulcer]], [[antiviral drug|antiviral]], [[neuro-protective]], [[anti-depressant]] and [[anti-coagulant]].<ref>{{cite journal |author1=Aslam, M.S. |author2=Ijaz, A.S. |series=Review Article |title=Phytochemical and ethno-pharmacological review of the genus ''Araucaria'' |journal=Journal of Tropical Pharmaceutical Research |volume=12 |issue=4 |year=2013 |pages=651–659 |doi=10.4314/tjpr.v12i4.31|doi-access=free }}</ref>
